Field Preparation, Sowing Time and Seed Inoculation: For good establishment, the field should be well levelled and free from weeds. Prepare a fine seedbed with 2–3 ploughings followed by planking. The best sowing time is from the last week of September to the first week of October. Before sowing, treat the seed with Rhizobium culture by slightly moistening the seed, mixing one packet of culture thoroughly, drying it in shade, and broadcasting the inoculated seed in standing water on the same day, preferably in the evening to protect the bacteria from sunlight. 

Seed Rate and Method of Sowing: Use 8 kg berseem seed/acre. In calm weather, broadcast in standing water; in windy conditions, sow in a dry field followed by light raking and irrigation. The seed should be free from chicory (kashni) and weed seeds, removed by soaking seeds in water and discarding floating seeds. For higher yield and fodder quality, mix 750 g mustard seed with berseem seed. Berseem can also be grown with oats (12 kg/acre) by broadcasting oats first, mixing with soil, irrigating, then broadcasting berseem in standing water. It may also be mixed with ryegrass by adding 2–3 kg ryegrass/acre with berseem or 1 kg ryegrass/acre with berseem + oats or berseem + sarson; mix ryegrass seed with moist soil, broadcast evenly, then broadcast berseem seed, lightly rake and irrigate.

Fertilizer Application and Manganese Deficiency Management: Apply 6 t FYM and 20 kg P (125 kg superphosphate)/acre at sowing. If FYM is not applied, use 10 kg N (22 kg urea) and 30 kg P (185 kg superphosphate)/acre. Superphosphate also supplies sulphur. When ryegrass is mixed with berseem, apply 10 kg N (22 kg urea)/acre after each cutting. Manganese deficiency may occur in coarse soils, especially after rice, showing yellow or grey mottling on leaves. Control it by spraying 0.5% manganese sulphate (1 kg in 200 L water/acre) 2–3 times at weekly intervals after cutting.

Weed Control and Irrigation Management: For weed control, if itsit (Trianthema portulacastrum) occurs, sow berseem with raya (mustard) to suppress it, or delay sowing to the second week of October to reduce its incidence. For irrigation, give the first irrigation within 3–5 days in light soils and 6–8 days in heavy soils after sowing. Afterwards, irrigate every 8–10 days in summer and 10–15 days in winter, depending on soil and weather. In sandy loam soils, use good quality water at sowing, then irrigate with alternate saline tubewell and canal water.

Harvesting and Seed Production: The first cutting is ready about 50 days after sowing; later cuttings are taken every 40 days in winter and 30 days in spring, giving 4–6 cuttings. Harvesting with a scythe saves about 60% labour. For seed production, take the last fodder cut early, depending on the climate and leave the crop for seed in the first fortnight of April for BL 42, BL 43 and BL 44, and the second fortnight of April for BL 10. Remove shaftal and kashni weeds and irrigate frequently during seed formation. Seed crops can also be sown after basmati rice in late November or in the first fortnight of January, giving 2–3 fodder cuttings before seed production. The average seed yield is about 2 q/acre. To increase yield, spray 2% potassium nitrate (2 kg/100 L water/acre) twice at weekly intervals from flowering, or 7.5 g salicylic acid in 100 L water/acre (dissolved in 225 ml ethyl alcohol).

Plant Protection: Insect pests: Black ants carry away germinating seeds; locate and destroy their nests. Bihar hairy caterpillar damages the crop in September–October and March–April by feeding on leaves; destroys nearby weeds, gutpatna, bathu, jangli palak and wild castor, which act as alternate hosts. Gram caterpillar (Helicoverpa armigera) damages the seed crop; avoid growing berseem seed fields near tomato, gram, late wheat, sathi moong, sathi mash and sunflower, or control the pest on those crops to prevent migration. Disease: Stem rot (Sclerotinia sclerotiorum) appears in January–February, causing basal stem rot and white cottony growth around wilted patches. Manage it by summer flooding to destroy sclerotia, cutting the crop and exposing soil to sunlight, and avoiding berseem in heavily infected fields for 3–4 years. By following these recommended agronomic and plant protection practices, you can achieve healthy crop growth, multiple fodder cuttings, and higher yield and quality of berseem fodder and seed.

Agrochemical compatibility refers to the ability of two or more pesticides, fertilizers, or plant growth regulators to be mixed together without causing adverse chemical reactions, loss of effectiveness, or damage to the paddy crop. Understanding compatibility is crucial for efficient pest and disease management in paddy cultivation, as it allows farmers to reduce the number of spray applications, save time, labor, and costs.

Understanding Chemical Compatibility:
When mixing agrochemicals, three main types of incompatibility can occur: (1) Chemical incompatibility - where chemicals react and form harmful compounds or precipitates, (2) Physical incompatibility - where the mixture separates, clumps, or forms sediments, and (3) Biological incompatibility - where the effectiveness of one or both chemicals is reduced. For paddy farmers in Haryana, it is essential to follow compatibility charts and manufacturer guidelines before tank mixing.

General Compatibility Guidelines for Paddy:

1. Insecticides with Insecticides: Most organophosphates (like Chlorpyrifos 20% EC) and synthetic pyrethroids (like Lambda-cyhalothrin 5% EC) are generally compatible. However, always conduct a jar test before large-scale mixing.

2. Fungicides with Insecticides: Many fungicides like Tricyclazole 75% WP (for blast disease) can be mixed with insecticides like Fipronil 5% SC (for stem borer), but alkaline fungicides should not be mixed with acidic insecticides.

3. Herbicides Separate: Post-emergence herbicides for paddy, such as Bispyribac-sodium 10% SC, should generally be applied separately as they may react with other chemicals and cause crop injury.

4. Avoid Mixing with Alkaline Solutions: Do not mix pesticides with lime, Bordeaux mixture, or other alkaline substances unless specifically recommended.

Jar Test Procedure:
Before mixing chemicals in the spray tank, always perform a jar test: Take a transparent jar and add water in the same proportion as your spray tank. Add chemicals in the correct sequence (wettable powders first, then emulsifiable concentrates, then soluble powders). Mix thoroughly and observe for 30 minutes. If you notice separation, precipitation, heat generation, or color change, the chemicals are incompatible.

Proper Mixing Sequence:

1. Fill spray tank half with clean water
2. Add wettable powders (WP) first while stirring
3. Add water-dispersible granules (WG) next
4. Add emulsifiable concentrates (EC) or suspension concentrates (SC)
5. Add soluble powders (SP) or soluble liquids (SL) last
6. Fill remaining water while continuously agitating
7. Add adjuvants or stickers if recommended

Important Precautions for Haryana Paddy Farmers:
September is typically the reproductive to maturity stage for paddy in Haryana. During this period, tank mixing should be done carefully. Never mix more than two chemicals unless you have verified compatibility. Use soft water for mixing, as hard water can cause precipitation. Always maintain proper agitation in the spray tank to prevent settling.

Safety Measures:
When handling and mixing agrochemicals, farmers must wear protective equipment including chemical-resistant gloves, face mask or respirator, safety goggles, full-sleeved shirt, long pants, and boots. Mix chemicals in well-ventilated areas, preferably outdoors. Never use bare hands to mix chemicals. If any chemical comes in contact with skin, wash immediately with soap and water. Store mixed solutions in labeled containers away from children and animals. Observe the Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI) of all chemicals used in the tank mix - always follow the longest PHI among the mixed chemicals. Dispose of empty chemical containers safely by triple rinsing and crushing them, never reuse them for domestic purposes.

For further guidance or clarification on specific chemical combinations for your paddy crop, farmers are advised to contact the nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) in Kaithal or local agricultural extension officer who can provide region-specific compatibility charts and recommendations.

Huminol is a humic acid-based organic product that can be effectively used in paddy cultivation as a soil conditioner and plant growth enhancer. Humic substances, including humic acid and fulvic acid, improve soil structure, nutrient availability, and overall plant health in rice farming systems.
 
 Benefits of Huminol in Paddy:
 Huminol enhances soil fertility by improving soil structure, water retention capacity, and cation exchange capacity. It chelates nutrients, making them more available for root uptake, particularly in waterlogged paddy conditions. Humic acid stimulates root development, leading to better nutrient and water absorption. It also increases the efficiency of applied fertilizers by reducing nutrient fixation and leaching losses, which is particularly valuable in flooded rice fields.
 
 Soil Testing and Nutrient Requirements:
 Before applying any soil amendments including Huminol, conduct soil testing to determine pH, organic carbon content, and available NPK levels. 

 Application Methods and Timing:
The recommended dose is 2.5 to 5 ml per lit. of water.

 Integration with Conventional Fertilizers:
 Combine Huminol with organic manures like Farm Yard Manure (FYM) at 5 tons per acre or vermicompost at 2.5 tons per acre for optimal results. Apply NPK fertilizers in split doses: nitrogen in 3 splits (50% basal, 25% at tillering, 25% at panicle initiation), phosphorus fully as basal, and potassium in 2 splits (50% basal, 50% at panicle initiation). Huminol enhances the efficiency of these fertilizers by improving their availability.
 
 Micronutrient Enhancement:
 Huminol improves the availability of micronutrients like zinc, iron, and boron, which are crucial for paddy. If soil tests indicate zinc deficiency (common in Tamil Nadu paddy fields), apply Zinc Sulphate at 25 kg per hectare ( 10 kg per acre) along with Huminol for better results.
 
 Safety Guidelines:
 
 Huminol is an organic product with minimal safety concerns. However, when handling concentrated liquid formulations, wear gloves to prevent skin irritation. Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Mix thoroughly with water before application to ensure uniform distribution. Avoid applying during heavy rainfall to prevent runoff losses.
 
 Expected Results:
 
 Regular use of Huminol in paddy cultivation can improve soil health over time, increase fertilizer use efficiency by 15-20%, enhance root growth and tillering, and potentially increase yields by 8-12% when combined with recommended fertilizer practices.
 
 For further guidance or clarification, farmers are advised to contact the nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or local agricultural extension officer.

ASD 16 and Co 51 are important paddy varieties developed for cultivation in coastal and salt-affected areas, particularly relevant for regions like Tamil Nadu where soil salinity is a significant challenge.
 
ASD 16 (Improved White Ponni) :
ASD 16 is a short-duration, salt-tolerant rice variety particularly suited for the Cauvery delta region and coastal areas of Tamil Nadu. This variety exhibits good tolerance to salinity during both germination and vegetative stages, making it suitable for areas with moderate salt stress. The variety matures in approximately 110-115 days and produces medium-slender grains with good cooking quality. ASD 16 can tolerate salinity levels up to 6-8 dS/m during the vegetative stage. The expected yield ranges from 23 quintals per acre under optimal management conditions. This variety responds well to proper fertilizer management and recommended spacing of 20 cm X 15 cm with 2-3 seedlings per hill.
 
Co 51 :
Co 51 is another salt-tolerant variety developed by Tamil Nadu Agricultural University, specifically bred for cultivation in coastal saline soils. This variety demonstrates excellent salt tolerance at the seedling stage and can withstand salinity levels up to 8-10 dS/m during early growth stages. Co 51 matures in about 105-110 days and is characterized by medium-bold grains with good grain quality. The variety yields approximately 26 quintals per acre under favorable conditions. It shows moderate resistance to major pests and diseases common in coastal regions.
 
Regional Suitability :
Both varieties are well-suited for the Thiruvarur district and other coastal districts of Tamil Nadu, including Nagapattinam, Thanjavur, and Cuddalore. They are primarily Kharif season varieties but can be grown in areas with assured irrigation during Rabi as well.

For salt-affected soils, apply 40-60 quintal of farmyard manure per acre before final land preparation to improve soil structure. The recommended NPK dose is 60:20:20 kg per acre for ASD 16 and 48:16:16 kg per acre for Co 51, applied in splits. Maintain a thin film of water (2-3 cm) during early stages and avoid water stagnation to minimize salt concentration in the root zone. Periodic drainage helps leach accumulated salts.
 
Key Advantages :
Both varieties offer farmers in salt-affected areas the opportunity to achieve reasonable yields where conventional varieties fail. Their salt tolerance, combined with acceptable grain quality and market demand, makes them economically viable options for coastal farming systems.

Root-eating insects in paddy nurseries are a significant concern for farmers, particularly during the early stages of crop establishment. These pests can severely damage the developing root system of young seedlings, leading to poor plant vigor, stunted growth, and reduced transplanting quality.
 
 **Description of Root-Eating Insects:**
 In paddy nurseries, common root-eating pests include white grubs (Holotrichia species), root aphids, wireworms, and root weevils. These insects feed on the tender roots of germinating seeds and young seedlings, causing direct damage to the underground plant parts. White grubs are particularly damaging as they are the larval stage of beetles and have strong mandibles that can completely sever roots.
 
 **Damage Symptoms:**
 Infested nursery beds show yellowing and wilting of seedlings despite adequate moisture. Plants become weak and can be easily pulled out due to damaged root systems. In severe cases, patches of dead or dying seedlings appear in the nursery. The seedlings may show stunted growth with reduced tillering capacity. Upon inspection of the soil, the presence of grubs or other root-feeding larvae can be observed near the root zone.
 
 **Severity Assessment:**
 The severity depends on pest population density and nursery conditions. Initial infestations may cause localized damage to small patches, while severe infestations can destroy entire nursery beds, necessitating re-sowing. Waterlogged conditions and presence of organic matter can attract these pests.
 
 **Control Measures:**
 
 *For Severe Infestations:*
 When damage is extensive, chemical control becomes necessary. Apply Quinalphos 25% EC at the rate of 2 ml per liter of water as a soil drench around the affected areas in the nursery bed. Alternatively, Chlorpyrifos 20% EC at 2.5 ml per liter of water can be used. Apply the solution directly to the soil in the evening hours when the pests are more active. The Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI) for these insecticides is 15-20 days, though in nursery management, this is less critical as seedlings are transplanted rather than harvested.
 
 *For Initial Stage/Preventive Management:*
 Before sowing, treat the nursery bed soil with neem cake at 250 kg per hectare or incorporate well-decomposed farmyard manure. Flood the nursery bed for 24 hours before sowing to drive out soil-dwelling insects. Practice crop rotation and avoid establishing nurseries in the same location repeatedly. Use light traps in the evening to attract and kill adult beetles that lay eggs in the soil. Biological control using entomopathogenic nematodes or Beauveria bassiana can be effective against soil-dwelling larvae.
 
 **Protective Gear (Mandatory for Chemical Application):**
 When applying chemical insecticides like Quinalphos or Chlorpyrifos, farmers must wear chemical-resistant gloves to prevent skin contact. A face mask or respirator is essential to avoid inhalation of vapors. Wear protective clothing including long-sleeved shirts and full-length pants. Use eye protection such as goggles or a face shield to prevent splashing. After application, wash hands thoroughly with soap and water. Avoid eating, drinking, or smoking during pesticide handling and application.
 
 **Safety Disclaimer:**
 Strictly follow the recommended dosage of 2 ml per liter - do not exceed this concentration as it may cause phytotoxicity and environmental harm. Observe the Pre-Harvest Interval of 15-20 days if applicable. Avoid spraying during windy conditions or when rain is expected within 6 hours. Do not mix different chemicals unless specifically recommended. Properly dispose of empty pesticide containers by puncturing and burying them away from water sources. Store pesticides in their original containers, away from children, animals, and food items. Keep emergency contact numbers of local health centers readily available.

Question: Information about root eating insect control in paddy nursery

answer: Root-eating insects are a serious problem in paddy nurseries, as they damage germinating seeds and young roots, leading to poor seedling growth. Important root-eating pests in paddy nursery include the termite, the root caterpillar, and the rice root weevil. Termite is a social insects living in colonies that mainly consist of workers. The worker termites are yellowish-white and wingless, and they damage the crop by feeding on germinating seeds and tender roots, resulting in poor plant stand and drying of seedlings. The root caterpillar is white in colour, similar to boiled rice. It lives inside the roots and feeds on them, due to which plants turn yellow and weak. The economic threshold level (ETL) of root caterpillar at the vegetative stage is 5 per cent infested plants. The rice root weevil (Echinocnemus oryzae) grub feeds on rice roots, causing stunted growth, poor tillering, and the appearance of dead plants in patches in the nursery. For cultural management, keep the nursery field and bunds free from grasses and weeds, destroy crop stubble, and ensure timely sowing. Maintain proper drainage to avoid excess moisture. Use balanced fertilizer doses and avoid excessive nitrogen. In termite-prone areas, avoid the use of fresh farmyard manure and green manure. Regular weekly crop surveillance is essential. For biological and preventive control of termites and other root-eating insects, apply neem cake @ 4 quintals per acre (for nursery: about 40–50 kg per 1000 m²), which gradually reduces termite incidence. Along with this, mix Beauveria bassiana 1.15% @ 1.0 kg per acre (for nursery: about 100–125 g) with 25–30 kg well-decomposed FYM per acre (for nursery: 3–5 kg FYM), sprinkle light water on the mixture, keep it in shade for 8–10 days, and then apply it uniformly in the soil before the last ploughing or final nursery bed preparation. This practice effectively controls termites and other soil-borne pests while conserving beneficial insects. When pest infestation crosses the economic threshold level, apply Chlorpyriphos 20% EC @ about 1.0 litre per acre through irrigation water to control termites and root caterpillars effectively (for nursery: prepare a drenching solution @ 2.5 ml Chlorpyriphos per litre of water and apply uniformly on nursery beds). Timely field sanitation, use of bio-control agents, and need-based chemical application together ensure healthy nursery seedlings and better crop establishment.

Nematode-infected plants are not only weakened, but their root systems are more susceptible to secondary infections by fungi or bacteria. Control measure:
Cultural control:
- Deep ploughing of fields during summer.
- Soil solarization: Cover the beds with polythene sheet of 45 gauge(0.45 mm) thickness for three weeks before sowing for soil solarization which will help in reducing the soil borne pests. 

Biological control:
- Apply neem cake/pongamia cake@ 100 kg/acre in soil at the time of last plouging or reducing nematodes, and soil dwelling pests.
- Apply Trichoderma spp. @ 2.5kg/acre along with FYM
 

 For specific recommendations or field-level diagnosis, please contact your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or Block Agriculture Officer.
 
 By following these steps, you can effectively manage nematode problems in your bottle gourd crop and ensure healthy plant growth and high yields.

Blossom end rot is a common issue in tomato plants, particularly during the flowering stage. This disorder is characterized by the development of dark, sunken lesions on the bottom of the fruit. Here are steps to manage and prevent blossom end rot: 

Blossom-end rot
Blossom end rot is a physiological disorder of tomato that can appear on fruits at any time in their development, but most commonly appears when fruits are one-third to one-half grown. The initial symptoms are water-soaked spots on the blossom end of the fruit. These spots later enlarge and become black. Secondary infection by other decay causing organisms usually follows. The cause of this disorder is considered to be calcium deficiency in the developing fruit. Extreme fluctuations in moisture, root pruning and excessive nitrogen fertilization can also result in blossom end rot.

Control: Avoid excessive application of Nitrogen particularly in ammonium form. Application of lime or calcium based fertilizers (eg. Calcium Ammonium Nitrate) as basal dose is commonly used to control this physiological disorder. Foliar spray of Calcium chloride (3 g/litre of water) also controls this disorder.

Nutrient Management: - Ensure that the soil is well-balanced with all essential nutrients During final land preparation, apply 10–12 tons of well-decomposed cow dung manure per acre, and at the time of planting, apply about 60 kg nitrogen (130 kg urea), 24 kg phosphorus (150 kg SSP), and 24 kg potash (40 Kg MOP) per acre.

For specific recommendations or field-level diagnosis, please contact your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or Block Agriculture Officer.

eMPOWER (Granules) is an organic soil amendment containing humic and fulvic acids that significantly enhances paddy growth and nutrient uptake. This product is particularly beneficial for improving soil health and plant development in rice cultivation.
 
 **Benefits of eMPOWER for Paddy:**
 The product contains humic and fulvic acids, which are natural organic compounds that stimulate root development in paddy plants. Enhanced root growth leads to improved nutrient absorption, better plant establishment, and increased overall vigor. These organic acids also improve soil structure, increase cation exchange capacity, and enhance the availability of nutrients already present in the soil. This results in more efficient utilization of applied fertilizers and better crop performance.
 
 **Application Method and Dosage:**
 For paddy cultivation, eMPOWER granules should be applied at a rate of 5-10 kg per acre. The lower dosage (5 kg/acre) is suitable for maintenance and moderately fertile soils, while the higher dosage (10 kg/acre) is recommended for poor soils or when maximum benefit is desired. The granules can be broadcast uniformly across the field before the final puddling operation or mixed with other organic amendments like farmyard manure.
 
 **Timing of Application:**
 For optimal results, apply eMPOWER granules during land preparation, ideally 7-10 days before transplanting. This allows the humic and fulvic acids to integrate with the soil and become available to young seedlings immediately after transplanting. In direct-seeded rice systems, apply the granules during the final land preparation and incorporate them into the soil.
 
 **Integration with Other Nutrient Management:**
 eMPOWER granules work synergistically with organic fertilizers such as farmyard manure (FYM), vermicompost, and green manure. When using eMPOWER, you can optimize chemical fertilizer use by following recommended NPK doses for paddy, typically 120:60:40 kg/ha (N:P:K), split-applied at basal, tillering, and panicle initiation stages. The improved nutrient uptake efficiency from eMPOWER may allow for slight reductions in chemical fertilizer doses over time.
 
 **Soil Testing Recommendations:**

The whitefly is widely distributed in tropical and subtropical regions, and in greenhouses in temperate regions. B. tabaci is highly polyphagous and is known to feed on several vegetables including tomato, eggplant and okra, and on field crops and weeds. Hot and dry conditions favor the whitefly, while heavy rain showers drastically reduce its population build-up. This insect is active during the day and settles on lower leaf surfaces at night.

Biology:
-Egg: Females lay roughly 300 small, pear-shaped eggs, often on the underside of hairy leaves near veins. Newly laid eggs are white, turning brown, and hatch in 3–5 days in summer or 5–33 days in winter.
-Nymph: Hatchlings, known as "crawlers," move to find feeding sites before settling down. Nymphs are flat, greenish-yellow, and feed on plant sap. They become immobile after the first stage, with the final stage (puparium) lasting 9–14 days in summer or 17–73 days in winter.
-Adult: These are soft-bodied, powdery white, moth-like insects that live for 1–3 weeks, with females slightly larger than males.
 
Damage symptoms:
-Both the adults and nymphs suck the plant sap and reduce the vigor of the plant.
- In severe infestations, the leaves turn yellow and drop off. 
-When the populations are high they secrete large quantities of honeydew, which favors the growth of sooty mould on leaf surfaces and reduces the photosynthetic efficiency of the plants.

Control Measures :
1.Monitoring and Sampling
Counting: Regularly count and record the number of both nymphs and adults on five randomly selected leaves per plant to track population levels.

2.Trapping Techniques
-Yellow Pan/Sticky Traps: Use these specifically for monitoring whiteflies.
-Quantity: Set up 10–12 traps per acre.
-Placement: Fix the traps 15 cm above the plant canopy for maximum effectiveness.
-DIY Option: You can make these locally by painting empty tins yellow and coating the outer surface with grease, Vaseline, or castor oil.

3.Biological Control (Natural Enemies)
-Parasitoids: Support or release species like Encarsia sp, Eretmocerus sp, and Chrysocharis pentheus (which targets the nymphal stage).

-Predators: Conserve natural hunters in the field, including:
Mirid bug (Dicyphus hesperus)
Dragonfly, spider, robber fly, and praying mantis
Fire ants and ladybugs (coccinellids)
Lacewings and big-eyed bugs (Geocoris sp)

4.Cultural & Habitat Management
-Border Crops: Plant maize, sorghum, or pearlmillet around the field edges to act as a barrier.
-Attractant Plants: Use specific plants to draw in beneficial insects:
-Cowpea: Attracts the parasitoid Eretmocerus hayati.
-French bean: Attracts predatory thrips that feed on whitefly.

 For specific recommendations or field-level diagnosis, please contact your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or Block Agriculture Officer.

Sulfur is an essential secondary macronutrient for wheat cultivation that plays a crucial role in protein synthesis, enzyme activation, and overall crop quality. In Punjab, particularly in districts like Gurdaspur, sulfur deficiency in wheat is increasingly common due to intensive cropping systems, reduced use of sulfur-containing fertilizers, and depletion of soil organic matter.
 
Before applying sulfur fertilisers, it is highly recommended to conduct soil testing through your nearest soil testing laboratory or Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK). Soil analysis will determine the actual sulfur status of your field and help you apply the right amount of fertiliser. Generally, soils with sulfur content below 10 ppm are considered deficient and require supplementation.
 
The sulphur fertiliser recommendation for wheat cultivation is to apply 100 kg of gypsum per acre or 18 kg of bentonite sulphur (90%) per acre before sowing to meet the sulphur requirement, especially in sandy soils or where phosphorus has been applied through DAP instead of single superphosphate. If the recommended dose of gypsum was already applied to the preceding groundnut crop, only 50 kg of gypsum per acre should be applied to wheat. In case sulphur deficiency is observed in the standing crop, gypsum can also be applied as a corrective measure, followed by irrigation.

Safety Considerations:
When handling sulfur fertilisers, wear gloves and avoid dust inhalation. Store fertilisers in a cool, dry place away from moisture. Follow recommended doses, as excessive sulfur can lower soil pH and affect nutrient availability.
 
For further guidance or clarification on soil testing procedures, fertiliser scheduling, or specific field conditions, farmers are advised to contact the nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or local agricultural extension officer in Gurdaspur district.

Caterpillar (locally known as 'sundi') is a significant pest problem in cotton cultivation in Rohtak and across Haryana. Several species of caterpillars attack cotton crops, including American bollworm (Helicoverpa armigera), spotted bollworms, tobacco caterpillar (Spodoptera litura), and pink bollworm (Pectinophora gossypiella). These pests cause substantial damage by feeding on leaves, squares, flowers, and developing bolls, leading to reduced yield and compromised fiber quality.
 
Spotted and pink caterpillars mainly attack the fruiting parts of cotton such as buds, flowers, and bolls from July to October. Infested fruiting bodies fall off and affected bolls become spindly and fail to develop properly. The attack is favoured by specific weather conditions—spotted caterpillar thrives around 24–26 °C with 95–100% humidity, while pink caterpillar prefers 20–23 °C with 52–72% humidity.

For prevention, farmers should regularly monitor crops and cut bent or drying branches and rose-like flowers affected by caterpillars twice a week, then collect and destroy them. Fallen or attached infested buds, flowers, and bolls should also be collected and buried deep or destroyed. American caterpillars should be collected manually and destroyed in insecticide-mixed water to reduce spread.

For chemical control, if infestation appears from late July to mid-August, spray any one recommended insecticide such as Quinalphos 25 EC @ 600ml in 150 to 175 litres of water per acre. If infestation of spotted or pink caterpillar occurs from mid-August to mid-October, then spray 80 to 100 ml Cypermethrin 25 EC in 175 to 200 litres of water and spray it per acre. But keep in mind that do not spray pesticides more than twice.

For further guidance or clarification, farmers are advised to contact the nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or local agricultural extension officer.

q_text:
Question: How to control caterpillar (sundi) in cotton crop in Rohtak, Haryana?

answer: Caterpillar (locally known as 'sundi') is a significant pest problem in cotton cultivation in Rohtak and across Haryana. Several species of caterpillars attack cotton crops, including American bollworm (Helicoverpa armigera), spotted bollworms, tobacco caterpillar (Spodoptera litura), and pink bollworm (Pectinophora gossypiella). These pests cause substantial damage by feeding on leaves, squares, flowers, and developing bolls, leading to reduced yield and compromised fiber quality.
 
Spotted and pink caterpillars mainly attack the fruiting parts of cotton such as buds, flowers, and bolls from July to October. Infested fruiting bodies fall off and affected bolls become spindly and fail to develop properly. The attack is favoured by specific weather conditions—spotted caterpillar thrives around 24–26 °C with 95–100% humidity, while pink caterpillar prefers 20–23 °C with 52–72% humidity.

For prevention, farmers should regularly monitor crops and cut bent or drying branches and rose-like flowers affected by caterpillars twice a week, then collect and destroy them. Fallen or attached infested buds, flowers, and bolls should also be collected and buried deep or destroyed. American caterpillars should be collected manually and destroyed in insecticide-mixed water to reduce spread.

For chemical control, if infestation appears from late July to mid-August, spray any one recommended insecticide such as Quinalphos 25 EC @ 600ml in 150 to 175 litres of water per acre. If infestation of spotted or pink caterpillar occurs from mid-August to mid-October, then spray 80 to 100 ml Cypermethrin 25 EC in 175 to 200 litres of water and spray it per acre. But keep in mind that do not spray pesticides more than twice.

For further guidance or clarification, farmers are advised to contact the nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or local agricultural extension officer.

Leucaena leucocephala, commonly known as Subabul or Leucaena, is a fast-growing leguminous tree that serves as an excellent green leaf manure crop and organic nutrient source for wheat cultivation. In Haryana's Fatehabad district and similar semi-arid regions, incorporating Leucaena into wheat farming systems can significantly improve soil health and crop productivity.

Benefits of Leucaena for Wheat Cultivation:
Leucaena is a nitrogen-fixing legume that can fix atmospheric nitrogen through symbiotic relationship with Rhizobium bacteria in root nodules. When incorporated into soil as green manure, it provides substantial amounts of nitrogen (approximately 150-200 kg N per hectare), phosphorus, and potassium. The fresh biomass contains around 3-4% nitrogen content, making it comparable to chemical fertilizers. Its deep root system brings up nutrients from lower soil layers, making them available for shallow-rooted wheat crops.

Cultivation Timeline and Method:
For wheat cultivation in Haryana, Leucaena should be grown as a border crop or in separate plots during the Kharif season. The tender leaves and twigs are harvested 30-45 days before wheat sowing (Sep-Oct)  for timely sown wheat in November). This 30-45 day period is crucial as it allows proper decomposition of the green biomass in soil, converting organic matter into plant-available nutrients before wheat planting.

Application Process:
Harvest young, succulent Leucaena branches and leaves when plants are 2-3 months old. Chop the material into 2-3 inch pieces for faster decomposition. Incorporate 8-10 tonnes of fresh Leucaena biomass per acre into the soil through ploughing. Apply the material 30-45 days before wheat sowing to ensure adequate decomposition. Add Trichoderma or other microbial decomposers at 2-3 kg per acre to accelerate the breakdown process. Maintain soil moisture after incorporation to facilitate microbial activity and decomposition.

Nutrient Contribution:
Leucaena green manure can supply approximately 40-50 kg nitrogen, 8-10 kg phosphorus, and 30-35 kg potassium per acre, reducing chemical fertilizer requirements by 25-30%. The organic matter improves soil structure, water retention capacity, and beneficial microbial populations. It also helps in maintaining soil pH and reducing problems of salinity and sodicity common in Haryana soils.

For further guidance or clarification on Leucaena cultivation, green manure application rates, or wheat fertilizer management, farmers are advised to contact the nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or local agricultural extension officer in Fatehabad district.

EC (Emulsifiable Concentrate) and SC (Suspension Concentrate) are two important pesticide formulations used in paddy cultivation, each with distinct characteristics and applications.
 
EC (Emulsifiable Concentrate) Formulation:
EC formulations are liquid pesticides that form a milky emulsion when mixed with water. They consist of the active ingredient dissolved in an organic solvent along with emulsifying agents. When added to water for spraying, the oil-based solution disperses to create a stable emulsion. EC formulations have been traditionally popular due to their effectiveness and ease of mixing. However, they contain organic solvents, which can be flammable and may cause phytotoxicity (plant damage) if not used properly. The solvent component can also pose environmental and health concerns.
 
SC (Suspension Concentrate) Formulation:
SC formulations are water-based suspensions containing finely ground solid particles of the active ingredient dispersed in water with suspending and dispersing agents. When added to spray water, these particles remain suspended, creating a stable mixture. SC formulations are a more modern development designed to overcome the limitations of EC formulations.
 
Key Differences:
 1. Solvent Base: EC uses organic solvents while SC uses water as the base, making SC more environmentally friendly.
 2. Flammability: EC formulations are flammable due to organic solvents, whereas SC formulations are non-flammable, making them safer to store and transport.
 3. Phytotoxicity Risk: SC formulations have a lower phytotoxicity risk compared to EC, as they lack harsh organic solvents that can damage plant tissues.
 4. Storage: SC formulations are generally more stable during storage and less prone to separation.
 5. Application Safety: SC formulations produce less odor and are less irritating to applicators compared to EC formulations.
 6. Environmental Impact: SC formulations are more eco-friendly as they don't release volatile organic compounds into the atmosphere.
 
Advantages of SC over EC for Paddy Cultivation:
For paddy farmers, SC formulations offer safer handling, reduced risk of crop damage, better environmental compatibility, and improved worker safety. They are particularly beneficial in paddy fields where water management is critical and environmental safety is a priority.
 
Protective Gear (When Using Either Formulation):
Regardless of formulation type, farmers must wear appropriate protective equipment, including chemical-resistant gloves, face masks or respirators, protective clothing covering arms and legs, and eye protection (goggles or face shield). Avoid spraying during windy conditions and never eat, drink, or smoke during application.
 
Safety Disclaimer:
Always follow label instructions for recommended doses and application rates. Observe the Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI) specified on the product label before harvesting. Store pesticides in original containers away from food, feed, and children's reach. Dispose of empty containers safely by triple rinsing and following local disposal guidelines. Never reuse pesticide containers for any other purpose.
 
For further guidance or clarification, farmers are advised to contact the nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or local agricultural extension officer.

Thrips are significant sap-sucking pests that can cause considerable damage to sugarcane crops, particularly during the early growth stages. These minute insects feed on plant sap by piercing the leaf tissues, resulting in characteristic silvery streaks, leaf curling, stunted growth, and reduced photosynthetic efficiency.

Identification and Damage Symptoms: Thrips (primarily Fulmekiola serrata and Scirtothrips dorsalis) are tiny, slender insects measuring 1-2 mm in length.  The thrips damage the crop from April to June. This pest sucks the sap from the partly opened leaf and tips of the younger leaves, resulting in withering and drying of leaf tip, which get rolled inwardly. The thrips prefer plant crop than ratoon crop.

Chemical Control Measures: Mix 500 ml of oxydemeton‑methyl 25 EC or 600 ml of Dimethoate 30 EC in 250 liters of water and spray it per acre.

Biological Control Methods: Encourage natural predators such as ladybird beetles, lacewings, predatory thrips (Montandoniola moraguesi), and parasitic wasps that naturally suppress thrips populations.

Cultural Management Practices: Implement crop rotation with non-susceptible crops to break the pest cycle. Remove and destroy heavily infested plant material to reduce thrips populations. Maintain proper field sanitation by controlling weeds that serve as alternate hosts. Ensure adequate irrigation and balanced fertilization to promote vigorous plant growth that can better withstand thrips damage. Plant resistant or tolerant sugarcane varieties where available. Monitor fields regularly, especially during dry weather when thrips populations typically increase.

Integrated Approach: Combining chemical, biological, and cultural methods provides the most sustainable and effective long-term management of thrips in sugarcane. Rotate different chemical groups to prevent resistance development and use chemical control only when thrips populations exceed economic threshold levels.

Cutworms are a common pest that can cause significant damage to barseem (Egyptian clover) crops. But as per POP, it is not major as well as devastating pest of barseem. Common major pest of barseem as per POP are ant and Gram Caterpillar.

Ants: These carry away the seeds even before they can germinate.

Control: Locate the nesting sites of these ants and dust them with recommended chemicals.

Gram Caterpillar (Helicoverpa): This insect destroys Berseem by consuming it in large quantities during April. During this period, more than 90% of the insects migrate from other crops to attack the Berseem fields.

Control: 
- Mix 400 ml of Malathion 50 EC in 300 liters of water and spray per acre.
- For crops intended as green fodder for livestock, use only Malathion. Wait at least 7 days after spraying before feeding this fodder to animals.
- If using a motorized knapsack sprayer, the amount of chemical remains the same as mentioned above, but the water quantity should be reduced to 1/10th.

Cultural Control:
 - Practice deep ploughing after the previous crop to expose and destroy overwintering cutworm pupae.
 - Use proper crop rotation, avoiding planting barseem after crops like maize, wheat or sorghum that can harbor cutworms.
 - Maintain good field sanitation by removing weeds and crop residues that can serve as alternative hosts.
 - Use row covers or mulches to create a physical barrier against cutworm entry.
 
 Monitoring and Timely Action:
 - Regularly inspect the field, especially the base of plants, for signs of cutworm damage.
 - Act promptly at the first signs of infestation to prevent significant crop losses.
 
 For specific recommendations or field-level diagnosis, please contact your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or Block Agriculture Officer.

Blight diseases in maize are significant fungal infections that can cause substantial yield losses if not managed properly. The two primary types are Turcicum Leaf Blight (Northern Corn Leaf Blight) caused by *Exserohilum turcicum* and Maydis Leaf Blight (Southern Corn Leaf Blight) caused by *Bipolaris maydis*.

Identification and Symptoms:
Large, long or oval brown spots on leaves
Severe infection causes drying of leaves

Integrated Management Strategy:

1. Cultural Practices:
- Use resistant or tolerant maize hybrids suitable for your region
- Practice crop rotation with non-host crops for 2-3 years
- Maintain proper plant spacing (60-75 cm between rows, 20-25 cm between plants) to ensure good air circulation
- Remove and destroy infected crop debris immediately after harvest
- Avoid excessive nitrogen application which promotes succulent growth
- Implement balanced fertilization with adequate potassium to improve plant resistance

Control Measures:
Zineb or Mancozeb 75% WP @ 800gm/acre; 
Ziram 80% @ 800 gm/acre mixed in 200-250 litres of water.

For specific recommendations or field-level diagnosis, please contact your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or Block Agriculture Officer.

Question: How can I identify and manage blight disease in maize?

answer: Blight diseases in maize are significant fungal infections that can cause substantial yield losses if not managed properly. The two primary types are Turcicum Leaf Blight (Northern Corn Leaf Blight) caused by *Exserohilum turcicum* and Maydis Leaf Blight (Southern Corn Leaf Blight) caused by *Bipolaris maydis*.

Identification and Symptoms:
Large, long or oval brown spots on leaves
Severe infection causes drying of leaves

Integrated Management Strategy:

1. Cultural Practices:
- Use resistant or tolerant maize hybrids suitable for your region
- Practice crop rotation with non-host crops for 2-3 years
- Maintain proper plant spacing (60-75 cm between rows, 20-25 cm between plants) to ensure good air circulation
- Remove and destroy infected crop debris immediately after harvest
- Avoid excessive nitrogen application which promotes succulent growth
- Implement balanced fertilization with adequate potassium to improve plant resistance

Control Measures:
Zineb or Mancozeb 75% WP @ 800gm/acre; 
Ziram 80% @ 800 gm/acre mixed in 200-250 litres of water.

Berseem (Trifolium alexandrinum), commonly known as Egyptian clover, is an important annual winter fodder crop widely cultivated for its high protein content and nutritional value for livestock. Proper fertilizer management is crucial for achieving optimal growth, quality forage production, and multiple cuttings throughout the season.
 
Recommended Fertilizer Dose:
The total fertilizer dose for Berseem cultivation depends on soil fertility status, variety, and expected number of cuttings. Generally, the recommended fertilizer application is:
 
- Apply 60 quintals of farmyard manure (FYM) along with 20 kg phosphorus (125 kg superphosphate) per acre at sowing time.
- Where farmyard manure has not been added, apply 10 kg nitrogen (22 kg Urea) and 30 kg phosphorus (185 superphosphate) per acre. The application of phosphorus in the form of superphosphate adds Sulphur.
- Where ryegrass has been mixed in berseem, apply 10 kg N (22 kg Urea) per acre after each cutting.
 
Micronutrients:
Manganese Deficiency: Manganese deficiency generally appears in coarse textured soils especially where berseem follows rice. The symptoms appear more prominently when the crop reaches the cutting stage. In the early stages of deficiency, the mid-stem leaves of berseem show grey to yellow mottling. Tip and about 1/3rd area from the base remains green. Later these mottling spreads on the entire leaf and color changes from pinkish to brown which coalesce to form necrotic lesions. Where the deficiency is noticed, spray the crop twice or thrice with 0.5% manganese sulphate solution (1 kg manganese sulphate in 200 liters of water per acre) at weekly intervals on sunny days. Spray the crop after two weeks of cutting
 
For further guidance or clarification, farmers are advised to contact the nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or local agricultural extension officer.

Sun scorch or leaf burn in cotton occurs when high temperatures (above 35–38°C, especially above 40°C) combine with low humidity, hot winds, and soil moisture stress, causing the plant to lose water faster than roots can absorb it; as a result, leaf edges turn yellow, then brown, dry, and brittle, leaves may curl, dry patches appear, and squares or young bolls may drop, mainly affecting the upper canopy exposed to direct sunlight. It should be distinguished from jassid (leafhopper) damage, where leaf edges yellow and curl downward (hopper burn), and from potassium deficiency, which usually starts on older leaves. Cotton is a warm-season crop needing a frost-free period of 180–240 days and grows best at 25–30°C, with a minimum of 15–20°C and maximum of 35–40°C; cool nights and 26–32°C during flowering and boll setting are ideal, and the crop requires bright sunlight, 50–100 cm rainfall, and irrigation where rainfall is below 50 cm, as temperatures above the optimum range and low moisture increase heat stress and leaf burn.

The key management step is proper water management by keeping soil moisture consistent, especially during flowering and boll formation, irrigating in early morning or late evening to reduce evaporation and avoid shock; if water is limited, use alternate furrow irrigation to maintain root moisture without waterlogging, use drip irrigation if available to prevent wet–dry cycles and leaf shedding, and apply straw or crop residue mulch between rows to lower soil temperature by 2–5°C and conserve moisture.

Balanced nutrition is essential during heat stress; avoid excess nitrogen as it increases sensitivity, ensure adequate potassium to regulate stomata and improve tolerance, and spray 1% potassium nitrate (2kg in 200 lit. of water)  or 0.5 to 1% (5 to 10 gm per lit. of water) 19:19:19 fertilizer for recovery. avoid pesticide sprays between 11 AM and 4 PM as droplets can cause burn—always spray in the early morning or late evening. Timely irrigation, balanced nutrition, mulching, and foliar sprays reduce sun scorch and help protect yield under heat stress.
For further guidance farmers are advised to contact the nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or local agricultural extension officer.

Question: How to manage sun scorch or leaf burn in cotton plants during high temperature stress?

answer: Sun scorch or leaf burn in cotton occurs when high temperatures (above 35–38°C, especially above 40°C) combine with low humidity, hot winds, and soil moisture stress, causing the plant to lose water faster than roots can absorb it; as a result, leaf edges turn yellow, then brown, dry, and brittle, leaves may curl, dry patches appear, and squares or young bolls may drop, mainly affecting the upper canopy exposed to direct sunlight. It should be distinguished from jassid (leafhopper) damage, where leaf edges yellow and curl downward (hopper burn), and from potassium deficiency, which usually starts on older leaves. Cotton is a warm-season crop needing a frost-free period of 180–240 days and grows best at 25–30°C, with a minimum of 15–20°C and maximum of 35–40°C; cool nights and 26–32°C during flowering and boll setting are ideal, and the crop requires bright sunlight, 50–100 cm rainfall, and irrigation where rainfall is below 50 cm, as temperatures above the optimum range and low moisture increase heat stress and leaf burn.

The key management step is proper water management by keeping soil moisture consistent, especially during flowering and boll formation, irrigating in early morning or late evening to reduce evaporation and avoid shock; if water is limited, use alternate furrow irrigation to maintain root moisture without waterlogging, use drip irrigation if available to prevent wet–dry cycles and leaf shedding, and apply straw or crop residue mulch between rows to lower soil temperature by 2–5°C and conserve moisture.

Balanced nutrition is essential during heat stress; avoid excess nitrogen as it increases sensitivity, ensure adequate potassium to regulate stomata and improve tolerance, and spray 1% potassium nitrate (2kg in 200 lit. of water)  or 0.5 to 1% (5 to 10 gm per lit. of water) 19:19:19 fertilizer for recovery. avoid pesticide sprays between 11 AM and 4 PM as droplets can cause burn—always spray in the early morning or late evening. Timely irrigation, balanced nutrition, mulching, and foliar sprays reduce sun scorch and help protect yield under heat stress.

Cultural practices form the foundation of successful paddy cultivation in Bhiwani district, Haryana, particularly during the Kharif season. These practices encompass land preparation, seedling management, transplanting, water management, and nutrient application that collectively ensure optimal crop growth and yield.
 
Land Preparation:
Proper land preparation is crucial for paddy cultivation in Haryana's semi-arid conditions. Begin with deep ploughing (15-20 cm) after the first monsoon rains to improve soil structure and water retention. Follow this with 2-3 harrowing operations to achieve a fine tilth. Puddling should be done thoroughly when the soil has adequate moisture, followed by levelling using a wooden plank or laser land leveller. Good levelling ensures uniform water distribution, which is critical in Bhiwani's water-scarce conditions.
 
Nursery Management:
For the Kharif season in Bhiwani, prepare nurseries in late May to early June. Use a seed rate of 10-12 kg/acre for nursery and then transplanting in the main field after 25-30 days. Apply well-decomposed farmyard manure (FYM) at 150-200 kg per nursery bed along with a basal dose of nitrogen and phosphorus. Ensure the nursery bed is kept moist but not waterlogged. Seedlings are ready for transplanting in 25-30 days when they reach 15-20 cm height.
 
Transplanting:
The optimal time for transplanting in Bhiwani is mid-June to early July, coinciding with the monsoon. Maintain a spacing of 20 x 15 cm or 20 x 20 cm, depending on the variety. Plant 2-3 seedlings per hill at a depth of 2-3 cm. Proper spacing ensures adequate sunlight penetration, air circulation, and nutrient availability, reducing disease and pest incidence.
 
Water Management:
Water is a critical constraint in the Bhiwani district. Maintain 5-7 cm of standing water during the vegetative and reproductive stages. During the tillering stage, practice intermittent irrigation to promote root development and reduce water consumption. Drain the field 10-15 days before harvest to facilitate harvesting operations and improve grain quality.
 
Nutrient Management:
 Soil testing is essential before nutrient application. Generally, for Haryana conditions, apply 60 kg nitrogen, 24 kg phosphorus, and 24 kg potassium per acre, which equals urea 130 kg, SSP 150 kg, and MOP 40 kg per acre, along with zinc sulphate (21%) @ 10 kg per acre. Apply the full dose of phosphorus, potash, and zinc, along with one-third nitrogen at transplanting, and split the remaining nitrogen into two equal doses at 3 and 6 weeks after transplanting (if basal nitrogen is missed, apply within 7 days). If DAP has been used, reduce the amount of urea by 20 kg.
 
Organic matter addition through FYM or compost at 6 tons per acre significantly improves soil health and water retention capacity. Green manuring with dhaincha (Sesbania aculeata) before transplanting adds nitrogen and improves soil structure.
 
For micronutrient deficiencies common in Bhiwani soils, apply zinc sulphate at 10 kg per acre if deficiency symptoms (brown spots on older leaves) appear. Iron deficiency can be corrected through foliar spray of ferrous sulphate (0.5%) solution.
 
Weed Management:
Cultural weed control includes maintaining standing water, hand weeding at 20 and 40 days after transplanting, and proper spacing. Early flooding after transplanting suppresses weed germination effectively.

KVK Referral:
For further guidance or clarification on cultural practices specific to your farm conditions, farmers are advised to contact the nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) in Bhiwani district or the local agricultural extension officer for soil-specific recommendations and demonstration of best practices.

The management of weeds in paddy cultivation is critical for achieving optimal yields, and herbicides like Pretilachlor 50% EC and Butachlor 50% EW are widely used pre-emergence herbicides for effective weed control in rice fields. Water Retention Requirement: After applying Pretilachlor 50% EC or Butachlor 50% EW in paddy fields, water should be maintained in the field for a minimum of 72 hours (3 days). This standing water is essential for the proper functioning of these herbicides, as they work by forming a chemical layer on the soil surface that prevents weed seed germination. The water acts as a carrier and helps in uniform distribution of the herbicide, ensuring effective weed suppression. Application Guidelines: These herbicides should be applied within 3-5 days after transplanting in transplanted paddy or within 2-3 days after sowing in direct-seeded rice. The field should have 2-5 cm of standing water at the time of application. The recommended dose is 600 ml per acre for Pretilachlor 50% EC and 1.2-1.6 litre per acre for Butachlor 50% EC, mixed in sufficient water (typically 200-250 liters per acre) for uniform spray coverage. Critical Water Management: Maintaining the 72-hour water retention period is crucial because if water drains out earlier, the herbicide layer breaks down, reducing its effectiveness significantly. Similarly, ensure that excess water does not flow out of the field during this period. After 72 hours, normal water management practices can be resumed. Do not drain the field immediately after this period; maintain shallow standing water as per standard paddy cultivation practices. Weed Control Spectrum: These herbicides effectively control annual grassy weeds like Echinochloa species (barnyard grass), Leptochloa, and broad-leaved weeds such as Ammannia, Ludwigia, and sedges like Cyperus species, which are common in paddy fields across Uttar Pradesh and other rice-growing regions.
PROTECTIVE GEAR (MANDATORY): When handling and applying these herbicides, farmers must wear: - Chemical-resistant gloves to protect hands - Face mask or respirator to avoid inhalation - Protective clothing including long-sleeved shirts and full-length pants - Eye protection such as goggles or face shield - Wash hands thoroughly with soap after application - Avoid eating, drinking, or smoking during application - Store herbicides in original containers, away from children, animals, and food items  
SAFETY DISCLAIMER: - Strictly follow the recommended doses; do not exceed the prescribed quantity - Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI): Observe a minimum of 60-70 days before harvest - Avoid spraying during windy conditions or when rain is expected within 24 hours - Do not mix different herbicides unless specifically recommended - Dispose of empty containers safely by puncturing and burying them away from water sources - Keep emergency contact numbers of local health centers handy - In case of accidental exposure, wash affected area immediately and seek medical attention Additional Precautions: Ensure proper leveling of the field before application for uniform water distribution. Avoid using contaminated water for irrigation during the 72-hour period. If manual weeding is needed later, wait at least 20-25 days after herbicide application. For further guidance or clarification, farmers are advised to contact the nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or local agricultural extension officer.

Top dressing is a critical fertiliser management practice in wheat cultivation that involves applying nitrogen fertiliser at specific growth stages after the initial basal application. In Uttar Pradesh, proper top dressing ensures vigorous vegetative growth, better tillering, and higher grain yield in wheat crops.
 
Understanding Top Dressing in Wheat:
Top dressing refers to the surface application of nitrogen fertilisers during active crop growth stages, primarily at the Crown Root Initiation (CRI) stage and tillering phase. This practice helps meet the crop's nitrogen demand during critical growth periods when nutrient uptake is maximum.
 
Recommended Top Dressing Schedule for Uttar Pradesh:
 
 For timely sown wheat (November), the typical fertiliser recommendation per acre is:
 - Nitrogen (N): 48 kg per acre (104 kg Urea)
 - Phosphorus: 24 kg per acre (150 kg SSP)
 - Potash: 16 kg per acre (27 kg MOP)

For Loam or Matyar, Kawar, and Mar, half of the quantity of nitrogen and the full quantity of phosphate and potash should be given 2-3 cm below the seeds in the furrows, and the remaining quantity of nitrogen should be given before 2 hours of the first irrigation.
 
The nitrogen application should be split as follows:
First Top Dressing (21-25 Days After Sowing - CRI Stage):
Apply 52 kg of Urea per acre (approximately half N). This coincides with the Crown Root Initiation stage, which is crucial for establishing a strong root system and promoting effective tillering. The CRI stage typically occurs 20-25 days after sowing when the first irrigation is given.

In sandy, loam,rakad and padwa sandy clay,1/3rd quantity of nitrogen and the full quantity of phosphate and potash should be given below the seeds in the furrows. Half of the remaining quantity should be given after the first irrigation, after 20-25 days of sowing at the crown root initiation stage, and the remaining quantity after the second irrigation. 

First Top Dressing (21-25 Days After Sowing - CRI Stage):
Apply 35 kg of Urea per acre. This coincides with the Crown Root Initiation stage, which is crucial for establishing a strong root system and promoting effective tillering. The CRI stage typically occurs 20-25 days after sowing when the first irrigation is given.

Second Top Dressing: (After 40-45 days of sowing (tillering stage)
Application Method and Precautions:
Apply 35 kg of Urea per acre. This coincides with the tillering stage.

 1. Soil Moisture: Always apply top dressing when soil has adequate moisture, preferably just before irrigation or within 1-2 days after irrigation. Never apply to dry soil.
 
 2. Broadcasting Technique: Broadcast the urea uniformly across the field. Ensure even distribution to avoid patchy growth.
 
 3. Avoid Leaf Contact: Do not apply when leaves are wet with dew or after rain, as urea can cause leaf burn. Apply during morning hours after dew dries or in late afternoon.
 
 4. Immediate Irrigation: If applied on dry soil, provide light irrigation within 2-3 days to prevent nitrogen losses through volatilisation.
 
 5. Weed Management: Ensure the field is weed-free before top dressing, as weeds compete for applied nutrients.
 
Additional Nutrient Considerations:
 - Zinc Deficiency**: If wheat leaves show interveinal chlorosis (yellowing between veins), apply Zinc Sulphate @ 10 kg per acre mixed with soil or 0.5% foliar spray.
 
 - Split Application Benefits: Splitting nitrogen application improves nitrogen use efficiency, reduces leaching losses, and synchronizes nutrient supply with crop demand.
 
 For further guidance on soil-specific fertilizer recommendations and soil testing facilities, please contact your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) in Firozabad district.

Understanding Pendimethalin Application:
Pendimethalin (30% EC) works by creating a chemical barrier in the soil that prevents weed seed germination. For effective weed control, it must be applied as a pre-emergence herbicide, meaning it should be sprayed within 1-2 days after sowing but before wheat and weed seeds germinate. The recommended dose is typically 1.5 liters per acre mixed in 200-250 liters of water.
 
Challenges with Broadcasting Method:
In the broadcasting sowing method, wheat seeds are scattered randomly on the soil surface rather than being placed in rows at uniform depth. This creates several challenges for pendimethalin application:
 
 1. Uneven Seed Depth: Seeds lie at varying depths, with many remaining on or near the soil surface. Pendimethalin can potentially affect wheat germination if seeds are not adequately covered with soil.
 
 2. Direct Contact Risk: Surface-lying wheat seeds may come in direct contact with the herbicide spray, increasing the risk of phytotoxicity and poor crop establishment.
 
 3. Reduced Selectivity: The herbicide's selectivity depends on wheat seeds being placed below the chemical barrier. Broadcasting disrupts this protective mechanism.

If you must use pendimethalin in broadcast-sown wheat, follow these precautions:
 
Soil Incorporation: After broadcasting wheat seeds, ensure thorough incorporation by using a light harrow or plank. This helps cover seeds with at least 2-3 cm of soil, creating a buffer between seeds and the herbicide.

 - Wear protective equipment including gloves, mask, goggles, and full-sleeved clothing
 - Avoid spraying during windy conditions to prevent drift
 - Maintain Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI) of 60-70 days before grain harvest
 - Dispose of empty herbicide containers safely by puncturing and burying
 - Wash hands and face thoroughly after application

The black coloration in mango flower parts is often indicative of anthracnose, a fungal disease or floral malformation  that can severely impact mango production. 

1. Anthracnose:

Disease symptoms:
• The disease causes serious losses to young shoots, flowers and fruits. It also affects fruits during storage.
• The disease produces leaf spot, blossom blight, wither tip, twig blight and fruit rot symptoms. Tender shoots and foliage are easily affected which ultimately cause ‘dieback’ of young branches. Older twigs may also be infected through wounds which in severe cases may be fatal.
• Depending on the prevailing weather conditions blossom blight may vary in severity from slight to a heavy infection of the panicles. Black spots develop on panicles as well as on fruits. Severe infection destroys the entire inflorescence resulting in no setting of fruits. Young infected fruits develop black spots, shrivel and drop off.
• Fruits infected at mature stage carry the fungus into storage and cause considerable loss during storage, transit and marketing.

Survival and spread:
• Fungus survives in dead twig and other host for long time which is the source of primary infection.

Favourable conitions:
• High humidity, frequent rains and a temperature of 24-32 °C favours the development of disease.

Cultural control:
• Diseased leaves, twigs, gall midge infected leaves and fruits, should be collected and burnt.
• Covering the fruits on tree, 15 days prior to harvest with news or brown paper bags.

Chemical control:
• Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 100 ml (0.1%)/100 litres of water depending on the size of the tree canopy or Copper oxychloride 50% WP @ 240 g ( 0.24%)/100 litres water as required depending upon PP equipment. For Anthracnose, spray Carbendazim 50% WP. Mix 400 to 800 grams of Carbendazim 50% WP in 400 to 800 liters of water per acre can be added in chemical treatment.

2.Mango malformation: 

There are two types of malformation symptoms namely:
1) Vegetative Malformation
2) Floral Malformation

Symptoms:
Vegetative Malformation: It is more commonly found on young seedlings. It is characterized by disrupting of apical growth resulting in several small flushes. The multi-branching of shoot apex with scaly leaves is known as "Bunchy Top" or "Witches' Broom". The malformed seedlings, remain stunted and die.
Floral Malformation: In malformation of inflorescense, shows variation in the panicle. Malformed head dries up in black mass and persist for long time.

Disease Development:
Disease spreads through propagating materials. The fungus does not sporulate insitu but sporulates on dried malformed panicles. The disease is severe at temperatures between 10-15 °C during December to January before flowering. Disease is mild in areas with 15-20 °C, sporadic between 20-25 °C. Plants at 4-8 years are susceptible. In some cases mites have been reported to be carrying the fungus and cause spread.

Management:
- Diseased plants should be destroyed.
- Use of disease-free planting material.
- Incidence reduced by spraying 100-200 ppm NAA during October.
- Pruning of diseased parts along the basal 15-20 cm apparently healthy portions.
 
 For specific recommendations or field-level diagnosis, please contact your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or Block Agriculture Officer.

 #### Protective Measures

 2. **Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI)**: Follow the PHI specified on the fungicide label to ensure that the fruit is safe for consumption.
 
 ### Integrated Pest Management (IPM)
 1. **Monitoring**: Regularly monitor the trees for signs of anthracnose to catch the disease early and implement control measures promptly.
 2. **Rotation of Fungicides**: Rotate fungicides to prevent the development of fungicide resistance.

Calcium deficiency in paddy fields can significantly affect crop growth, grain quality, and overall yield. Understanding and addressing this nutritional disorder is crucial for successful paddy cultivation, particularly in Tamil Nadu's Cuddalore district.
 
 **Introduction to Calcium Requirements:**
 Calcium is an essential secondary nutrient that plays a vital role in cell wall formation, root development, and nutrient uptake in paddy plants. Deficiency symptoms include stunted growth, poor root development, distorted young leaves with brown tips, and reduced tillering. The grain quality may also deteriorate with inadequate calcium availability.
 
 **Soil Testing Recommendations:**
 Before applying any calcium amendments, conduct soil testing through your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra or agricultural department laboratory. Soil testing will determine the exact calcium status, pH level, and other nutrient imbalances. This ensures precise nutrient management and prevents wasteful application.
 
 **Organic Calcium Sources:**
 For sustainable calcium management, incorporate organic sources such as:
 - Well-decomposed Farm Yard Manure (FYM) at 12-15 tonnes per hectare before final land preparation
 - Vermicompost at 5-6 tonnes per hectare, which improves calcium availability
 - Green manure crops like Sesbania or Dhaincha, which enhance soil structure and nutrient cycling
 - Wood ash (rich in calcium carbonate) at 2-3 tonnes per hectare
 
 **Chemical Calcium Amendments:**
 For immediate correction of calcium deficiency, apply:
 - **Agricultural Lime (Calcium Carbonate):** 200-250 kg per hectare, broadcasted and incorporated into soil 2-3 weeks before transplanting. This also helps correct soil acidity.
 - **Gypsum (Calcium Sulphate):** 200-300 kg per hectare for neutral to alkaline soils, applied at the time of final land preparation
 - **Calcium Nitrate:** 25-30 kg per hectare as foliar spray (0.5% solution) during active tillering and panicle initiation stages
 
 **Application Timing and Method:**
 Apply basal calcium amendments during land preparation to allow proper incorporation. For standing crops showing deficiency symptoms, foliar application of Calcium Nitrate or Calcium Chloride (0.5% solution) can provide quick relief. Apply foliar sprays during early morning or late evening hours.
 
 **Integrated Nutrient Management:**
 Maintain balanced NPK fertilization along with calcium. For paddy in Tamil Nadu conditions, apply 150:50:50 kg NPK per hectare in split doses. Ensure adequate organic matter incorporation to improve calcium retention and availability.
 
 **Safety Guidelines:**
 When handling calcium fertilizers:
 - Wear protective gloves and face mask during application
 - Avoid direct contact with skin and eyes
 - Store fertilizers in dry, cool places away from moisture
 - Follow recommended doses to prevent nutrient imbalances

q_question: How can I manage calcium deficiency in my paddy field?
q_text:
Question: How can I manage calcium deficiency in my paddy field?

answer: Calcium combines with pectin in the plant to form calcium pectate, which is an essential constituent of the cell-wall. It also promotes the activity of soil bacteria concerned with the fixation of free nitrogen or the formation of nitrates from organic forms of nitrogen. Furthermore, it is necessary for the development of a good root system. 

Calcium deficiency symptoms include white or bleached, rolled, and curled tips of the youngest leaves, necrosis along the lateral margins of the leaves, browning and death of older leaves, and stunting followed by death of the growing points. 

To prevent calcium deficiency, apply calcium containing fertilizer like gypsum based on soil test recommendations. Apply gypsum in Ca deficient high pH soils, such as sodic and high potassium soils. Apply farmyard manure or straw (either incorporated or burned) to compensate for calcium removal in soils that contain low levels of calcium, along with the application of calcium fertilizers based on soil test recommendations. Apply lime on acid soils to raise pH and Ca availability based on soil test.  TNAU POP recommends using 200 kg gypsum/acre in calcium deficient high pH soils. If calcium deficiency symptoms occur in standing crop, apply 1% CaCl2 (Calcium Chloride) i.e.10 g/liter of water as foliar spray.

Plant protection is crucial for successful moong (green gram) cultivation in Punjab, particularly in regions like Mansa district. Moong crops face multiple pest and disease challenges that require integrated management approaches for optimal yield.
 
 Major Pests  and Management of Moong:
 
 Whitefly: Nymphs and adults of whitefly suck sap from the leaves, thus lowering the vitality of the plants. Whitefly excretes honeydew on which sooty mould develops, resulting in blackening of leaves and decrease in the normal photosynthesis. In case of severe attack, there is total blackening of the crop, resulting in drying of leaves and ultimately total crop failure. Whitefly is a vector of mungbean yellow mosaic virus. Spray the crop upon pest appearance with 1.0 litre of homemade neem extract using 80-100 litres of water per acre with manually operated knapsack sprayer. To prepare neem extract, boil 5.0 kg mixture of neem leaves and fruits in 10 litres of water for 30 minutes. Then, filter this material through muslin cloth and use the filterate for spraying at the recommended dose. Repeat the spray after one week. Spray Pyriproxyfen 10 % + Bifenthrin10 % w/w EC @400ml in 200 liters of water.


Pod sucking bug (Clavigralla gibbosa): The adults are brown-grey in colour. Both 
nymphs and adults use their mouthparts to pierce the pod wall and suck the sap from the developing seeds. The attack is noticeable from the white patches that appear on the surface of pods and leaves. As a result of continuous sap feeding, premature drying of pods is noticed. When such pods are opened, shriveled and malformed seeds are observed. Further, such seeds easily succumb to secondary infection by fungal pathogens and pose problems in post harvesting process. Seeds spoiled by the pod bug neither germinate nor are acceptable as human food. 
To control this pest, spray the crop upon pest appearance at podding stage with 1250 mL  of homemade neem extract using 80-100 litres of water per acre with manually operated knapsack sprayer. Repeat the spray after one week, if necessary.

Tobacco caterpillar (Spodoptera litura): It is a polyphagous pest. The small larvae are 
black whereas grown up larvae are dark green with black triangular spots on body. Its’ moth lays eggs in masses covered with brown hairs on the lower side of leaves. After hatching, first and second instar larvae feed gregariously and skeletonize the foliage. Later on, the grown up larvae disperse and feed singly. Besides leaves, they also damage buds, flowers and pods. For management, egg masses and young larvae of tobacco caterpillar feeding gregariously should be collected along with leaves and destroyed. Spray Chlorantraniliprole 47.85 % w/w SC @ 17 ml/acres in 160-240 liters of water.

Pod borer (Helicoverpa armigera): The larvae damage the crop by feeding on leaves, 
flower buds, flowers, pods and seeds in the pods, thus causing heavy loss in yield. The larvae may be pale green, yellow, brown or black in colour measuring about 3-5 cm in length when fully grown. Larval presence can be observed from damage to plant and from dark green faeces below the plants on the soil. The larvae fall on the ground when plants are shaken vigorously. spray Chlorantraniliprole 18.50 % SC @ 50 ml in 160-240 liters of water.

Hairy caterpillar: The body of the caterpillar is covered with hair. The caterpillar 
eats the green matter of leaves, leaving behind only the midribs. The crop may be totally denuded due to severe attack. When young, they feed gregariously but on few plants in scattered spots. Since, the young larvae are gregarious, they can be destroyed by pulling out the infested plants along with larvae and burying them underground. The grown up caterpillars can be destroyed by crushing them under feet or by picking and putting them into kerosenized water. For control  irrigate once to avoid prolonged mid-season drought to prevent pre-harvest, Dig the trenches of 1 inch depth between the fi elds & dust the trenches to kill the larvae in pits infestation.

Major Diseases and Management of Moong:

 Yellow mosaic virus: It is a viral disease transmitted by whitefly and is more severe on kharif moong. The leaves of the diseased plants develop irregular yellow and green patches. Infected plants bear no or only a few pale pods. Rogue out the diseased plants early in the season. Grow yellow mosaic virus tolerant varieties of moong, ML 1808, ML 2056 and ML 818. 

Cercospora leaf spot: It is caused by Cercospora cruenta and C. canescens. The disease spots are circular, brown and necrotic which coalesce to cover bigger area and cause defoliation. Intermittent rains are favourable for disease development. Grow disease resistant varieties of moong, ML 1808, ML 2056 and ML 818. Early planting i.e. immediately after onset of monsoon. Grow crop on bower system to avoid soil contact. Maintain proper drainage in the field. Spray Metiram 55% + Pyraclostrobin 5% WG @ 600-700 g in 200 liter of water having PHI -18 days. 

Root rot: Root rot caused by Macrophomina phaseolina produces dark lesions on leaves, branches, stems and roots. The tissue of the affected portion become weak and shred easily. Pycnidia can be seen on the affected portion. Plant in well-draining soils. Prepare seed beds to enhance rapid germination. Proper irrigation is provided to prevent flooding and saturated soil conditions. Soil amendment with farm yard manure @ 5 tonnes/acres.

 Anthracnose: It is caused by Colletotrichum lindemuthianum. Dark brown spots (horse shoe shaped) appear on the leaves and other parts of the plant. Under severe conditions lesions rapidly coalesce to girdle stems, branches, peduncles and petioles. Early planting i.e. immediately after onset of monsoon. Grow crop on bower system to avoid soil contact. Maintain proper drainage in the field. Seed treatment with Trichoderma viride1% WP @ 4g per Kg seeds.

 Bacterial leaf spot: Bacterial leaf spots caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. phaseoli are circular to irregular and brown. Use disease free seed. Moong varieties ML 1808, ML 2056 and ML 818 are fairly resistant/ tolerant to this disease. 


 **Application Guidelines:**
 - Begin monitoring from 15 days after sowing
 - Apply chemical sprays only when pest population exceeds Economic Threshold Level (ETL)
 - Ensure complete plant coverage during spraying
 - Spray during early morning or evening hours
 - Rotate chemical groups to prevent resistance development
 - Maintain minimum 7-10 days interval between consecutive sprays
 
 **SAFETY PRECAUTIONS:**
 Always wear protective clothing, gloves, and masks during pesticide application. Avoid spraying during windy conditions. Do not eat, drink, or smoke while handling chemicals. Store pesticides in original containers away from children and animals. Follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI) strictly before harvesting. Dispose of empty containers safely.

 For field-specific recommendations, pest identification, and demonstrations of integrated pest management practices, please contact your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK). KVK Mansa provides diagnostic services, soil testing, and season-specific advisory services tailored to local conditions. They can guide you on the most effective and economical pest management strategies for your moong crop.
